approach.help: Our foundation is here to help.

what_we_do.title_html: Programs where teachers learn to build lessons on curiosity, inquiry and projects
what_we_do.lead_html: Our programs are about teaching <mark>today</mark>: a teacher’s and a coordinator’s work in a world full of distractions, where a school competes for a child’s attention and interest every day. We help teachers win that attention back with the lesson itself, and coordinators build teams where such teachers want to stay.
what_we_do.lead_2_html: We don’t have a new pedagogy to sell. We use well-studied approaches we trust, train teachers to use them well, and show how AI can lighten the load.
what_we_do.stipend: Participants receive a stipend for both the training and the practice with children: teachers have more than enough work without us.
what_we_do.practice_note: 10+ lessons for teachers to try it on real children

how_it_works.heading: How the program works

steps.title: Intensive
steps.body_html: Theory and workshops first: we take practical teaching methods apart, try them, and see what happens.

steps.title: Clubs
steps.body_html: We organise children’s clubs and gather the groups: <mark>over half the program</mark> happens there. For several weeks you lead sessions and try what we worked on together.

steps.title: Mentor
steps.body_html: <mark class="blue">Every week, in a small group,</mark> you go over your sessions with a mentor. The mentor stays with the group for the whole stretch of practice.

steps.title: Your class
steps.body_html: What works, you bring back to your own classroom. That is what the whole program is for.

how_it_works.note: Coordinators go through the same four steps; their practice is real cases from their own schools rather than clubs.

fellowship.title_html: Dear teachers,
intro: You see the effects of years of classroom disruption better than anyone. We want to give you time to learn, try things out, and work through what happens in the classroom with a mentor.
Morim Fellows, our program for teachers, starts with the later years of primary school and the beginning of middle school — when many children begin to lose interest in learning.

benefits.title: Specific teaching practices
benefits.body: In the intensives we take practical teaching methods apart, try them, and see what happens.
questions: “how do you get a class’s attention without raising your voice?”
“how do you build motivation that doesn’t depend on grades?”
“how do you start a lesson with a real question?”
“how do you get children to look for answers themselves instead of trying to guess what the teacher wants to hear?”

benefits.title: Practice with children in a safe setting
benefits.body: After the intensive, we organise clubs where you lead sessions with children for several weeks, trying out what we worked on together. Every week you go over your sessions with a mentor. A club is low stakes: no fear of getting it wrong in front of your own class. The point is to bring what works back to your classroom.
benefits.prose_html: We organise the clubs and gather the groups. For several weeks you lead sessions with children and go over each one with a mentor. No fear of getting it wrong in front of your own class, and what works, you bring back to it.

benefits.title: A stipend for your time
benefits.body:
You have more than enough work without us, so we pay participants a stipend for both the training and the practice with children.
If we believe a teacher’s time matters, it makes sense to act like it.

intro: Strong teachers need schools where they can do good work and want to stay. That’s why we work with teachers at more than one level: in their own classrooms and in the teams they help lead.
Morim Leaders, our first program for coordinators, is being developed together with rakazim themselves. The first pilot is under way with a closed cohort.

benefits.title: Leading without formal authority
benefits.body:
Rakazim are teachers too. They teach their own classes and help a whole team work better, often without formal authority over the people they lead.
How do you move a team forward when the people in it don’t report to you?

benefits.title: Feedback that actually helps
benefits.body:
How do you give feedback that people can use, support colleagues, and help them grow?
Participants bring real situations from their schools and work through them together with a mentor.

benefits.title: Making room for the work that matters
benefits.body:
How do you distribute the workload across the team and still make time for professional growth — yours and your colleagues’?
The program also covers the practical systems and projects that keep a department running without letting coordination take over the time meant for teaching.

results: Our first intensive in Tbilisi focused on inquiry-based education. We surveyed the same teachers twice: after the intensive, and again after several weeks of teaching children with weekly mentoring.

Teachers’ responses changed noticeably after practice. On the fundamentals — what an inquiry lesson is for, how it differs from a merely engaging one, and what the teacher does — the share of answers at “I understand and can use it” rose from 40% to 81%. Fewer teachers reported being worried about having to adapt when a lesson went off plan.
tbilisi.quote: “I’ve become noticeably less inclined to steer children toward the right answer, and more attentive to how they reason.”
tbilisi.quote_note: One of the teachers · that’s the change we’re looking for
results_after: Not everything became easier. Group dynamics remained difficult, and we’re adding more practice and mentoring around it.
Three-quarters of the children surveyed said they would like lessons like these at school.
tbilisi.caveat: Encouraging results, but still from a small group in an unusually friendly setting. We’ll see how they hold up in regular classrooms.

partners.title: For schools and partners
partners.lead: We run our programs with partners: schools that host an extracurricular, organisations that already work with children, and municipalities that want the programs for their own teachers. We are looking for places to practice and people to practice with, not funding.

types.title: Schools
types.body: A fellow runs an after-hours club with your children during the practice weeks. You give a room, a group, and a contact person; we bring the program, the mentor, and the stipend.

types.title: Organisations that work with children
types.body: After-school programs, camps, and youth centres can host practice weeks and gain a trained teacher for a season.

types.title: Municipalities and networks
types.body: Bring the programs to your own teachers and coordinators, cohort by cohort, with practice in your schools.

note.title: The team
note.body: We bring together teacher-development specialists and practicing teachers. We’re also building a circle of experienced Israeli educators and researchers who can tell us when we’re wrong and help us understand the school system from the inside.

questions.a: We currently focus on practicing teachers in Israel, in the later years of primary school and the beginning of middle school. If you work with another age group, you can still get in touch and tell us about your experience.

We teach teachers to use AI — and to teach children how to use it — instead of training AI to replace teachers. Good pedagogy has always been <mark>costly</mark>. New technology lets us widen its reach.
Theory and workshops are mixed with practice throughout. Teachers work with children; coordinators bring real situations from their schools. Both meet in small groups with a mentor every week.
Yes. Both teachers and coordinators receive a stipend. The amount and payment arrangements will be provided with the details of each program.

questions.q: Can a school or municipality work with Morim?
questions.a: Yes. We’re interested in working with schools, networks, and municipalities that want to bring our programs to their teachers or coordinators. We’re also looking for experienced educators who can help us build the programs. Read about partnering with us.
